And what, monks, is the power of development? Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhana, which is accompanied by thought (vitakka) and examination (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion. With the subsiding of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhana, which has internal confidence and singleness of mind, is without thought and examination, and has rapture and happiness born of concentration (samādhi). With the fading away as well of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences happiness with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhana of which the Noble Ones declare: 'He is equanimous, mindful, and dwells happily.' With the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhana, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, monks, is called the power of development. Monks, these are the two powers.

This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this:

“The trainee and the one beyond training in this world,
Are worthy of gifts for those who sacrifice.
They are upright in body, speech, and mind.
They are the field for those who sacrifice;
A gift given to them yields great fruit.”

37. Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Monastery. At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Monastery, the palace of Migāra's mother. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the monks: “Friends, monks.” “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:

“Friends, I will teach you about the person with internal fetters and the person with external fetters. Listen and attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta taught this:

“And what, friends, is the person with internal fetters? Here, friends, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them.”
65:
That monk, with the breaking up of the body, after death, arises in one of the deva realms (among the six sensual deva realms). When he passes away from that deva world, because he returns to this world through rebirth, he is called a returner (āgāmī), one who returns to this lower realm. Friends, this person is called a returner bound by internal fetters (ajjhattasaṃyojano), because he returns to this human world through rebirth.

Friends, what is the person bound by external fetters? Friends, here in this teaching, a monk is virtuous. He dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, accomplished in conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), seeing danger in the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the training rules. He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna attainment, which is the stilling of defilements and the liberation of the mind from defilements, being one of the eight attainments. With the breaking up of the body, after death, he arises in one of the Brahma realms (among the five Pure Abodes). When he passes away from that realm, because he does not return to this human world through rebirth, he is called a non-returner (anāgāmī). Friends, this person is called a non-returner bound by external fetters (bahiddhāsaṃyojano), because he does not return to this human world through rebirth.

Furthermore, friends, a monk is virtuous... [pe]... he trains in the training rules. He practices for disenchantment with, for dispassion toward, and for the cessation of sensual pleasures. He practices for disenchantment with, for dispassion toward, and for the cessation of the three types of existence. He practices for the destruction of craving for sensual pleasures. He practices for the destruction of greed for existence. With the breaking up of the body, after death, he arises in one of the Brahma realms (among the five Pure Abodes). When he passes away from that realm, because he does not return to this human world, he is called a non-returner (anāgāmī). Friends, this person is called a non-returner bound by external fetters (bahiddhāsaṃyojano), because he does not return to this human world through rebirth.

Then, many deities of equal mind approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, those deities said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is teaching the monks about the person bound by internal fetters and the person bound by external fetters at the Palace of Migāra’s Mother (Visākhā) in the Eastern Monastery. Venerable Sir, the assembly is delighted. Venerable Sir, we request that the Blessed One approach the Venerable Sāriputta out of compassion.' The Blessed One consented by silence.
66:
Then, just as a strong man might extend his flexed arm or flex his extended arm, the Blessed One disappeared from the Jeta’s Grove and appeared before the Venerable Sāriputta at the Palace of Migāra’s Mother (Visākhā) in the Eastern Monastery. Having paid homage to the Blessed One, the Venerable Sāriputta sat to one side, and the Blessed One said this to him:

'Sāriputta, here many deities of equal mind approached me, paid homage to me, and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sāriputta, those deities said this to me: "Venerable Sir, the Venerable Sāriputta is teaching the monks about the person bound by internal fetters and the person bound by external fetters at the Palace of Migāra’s Mother (Visākhā) in the Eastern Monastery. Venerable Sir, the assembly is delighted. Venerable Sir, we request that the Blessed One approach the Venerable Sāriputta out of compassion."

Sāriputta, those deities and Brahmas, even in a space as small as the point of an awl, stand in groups of ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty, and they do not crowd one another. Sāriputta, the thought might occur: "Surely, it is because those deities have developed their minds in such a way that they can stand in groups of ten... sixty in a space the size of an awl’s point without crowding one another." But, Sāriputta, it should not be seen like that. It is right here in this teaching that those deities have developed their minds in such a way that they can stand... [pe]... without crowding one another. Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train yourselves thus: "We will have peaceful faculties and a peaceful mind." Thus, Sāriputta, you should train. Sāriputta, for you who have peaceful faculties and a peaceful mind, your bodily actions will be peaceful, your verbal actions will be peaceful, and your mental actions will be peaceful. We will offer only peaceful offerings of body, speech, and mind to our fellow practitioners. Thus, Sāriputta, you should train. Sāriputta, those wanderers of other sects who have not heard this Dhamma discourse are ruined and lost.'

38. Thus have I heard. At one time, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying on the bank of the Bhaddasāri River in Varaṇā. Then the Brahmin Ārāmadanda approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna and exchanged friendly greetings with him.
67:
After exchanging pleasant and memorable greetings, the Brahmin Ārāmadanda sat to one side. Seated there, the Brahmin Ārāmadanda said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: "Venerable Kaccāna, what is the cause, what is the reason, why Khattiyas quarrel with Khattiyas, Brahmins quarrel with Brahmins, and householders quarrel with householders?"

"Brahmin, it is because of being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to sensual lust (kāmarāga) that Khattiyas quarrel with Khattiyas, Brahmins quarrel with Brahmins, and householders quarrel with householders."

"But Venerable Kaccāna, what is the cause, what is the reason, why ascetics (samaṇas) quarrel with ascetics?"

"Brahmin, it is because of being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to lust for views (diṭṭhirāga) that ascetics quarrel with ascetics."

"Venerable Kaccāna, is there anyone in the world who has transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to sensual lust, and who has also transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to lust for views?"

"Brahmin, there is such a person in the world who has transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to sensual lust, and who has also transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to lust for views."

"But who is that person, Venerable Kaccāna, in this world who has transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to sensual lust, and who has also transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to lust for views?"

"Brahmin, in the eastern districts, there is a city named Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, is currently staying. Indeed, Brahmin, that Blessed One has transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to sensual lust, and has also transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to lust for views."

When this was said, the Brahmin Ārāmadanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, uttered this inspired exclamation three times:

"That Blessed One has indeed transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to sensual lust, and has also transcended this being fettered, bound, obsessed, enslaved, and attached to lust for views."
68:
"Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One. [Repeated] Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One."

"Excellent, Venerable Kaccāna! Excellent, Venerable Kaccāna! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or hold up a lamp in the dark so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been clarified in many ways by the Venerable Kaccāna. I go to the Blessed One Gotama for refuge, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha. May the Venerable Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last."

39. On one occasion, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying at Madhurā in the Gundā Grove. Then the Brahmin Kandarāyana approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, after exchanging greetings, sat to one side. Seated there, the Brahmin Kandarāyana said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:

"Venerable Kaccāna, I have heard it said: 'The ascetic Kaccāna does not salute, rise for, or offer a seat to Brahmins who are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage.' Venerable Kaccāna, is this really so? For indeed, the Venerable Kaccāna does not salute, rise for, or offer a seat to Brahmins who are old, aged, burdened with years, advanced in life, and come to the last stage. Venerable Kaccāna, this is certainly not proper."

"Brahmin, the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Rightly Self-Awakened One, has declared the stage of an elder (vuddhabhūmi) and the stage of a youth (daharabhūmi). Even if one is eighty, ninety, or a hundred years old by birth, if he still indulges in sensual pleasures, dwells among sensual pleasures, is consumed by the fever of sensual pleasures, is devoured by sensual thoughts, and is eager in the pursuit of sensual pleasures, then he is reckoned as a foolish youth, not an elder."
69: Brahmin, even if a person is young, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, if he does not consume or enjoy sensual pleasures, does not live as a master in the house of sensual pleasures, is not burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, is not bitten by thoughts of sensual pleasures, and does not strive in the pursuit of sensual pleasures, then that person is indeed reckoned as a wise elder. When this was said, the Brahmin Kandarāyana rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and bowed his head at the feet of the young monks, saying: "Venerable sirs are elders, established in the stage of elders. We are young, established in the stage of the young." "Magnificent, Master Kaccāna! ... May Master Kaccāna accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts." 40. Monks, at the time when thieves are strong, kings are weak. At that time, monks, it is not easy for the king to enter or leave the city, or to tour the border districts. At that time, it is also not easy for Brahmins and householders to enter or leave the city, or to look after their external affairs. Even so, monks, at the time when bad monks are strong, the virtuous monks are weak. At that time, monks, the virtuous monks remain silent in the midst of the Saṅgha or live in the border districts. This, monks, is for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many, of devas and humans. Monks, at the time when kings are strong, thieves are weak. At that time, monks, it is easy for the king to enter or leave the city, or to tour the border districts. At that time, it is also easy for Brahmins and householders to enter or leave the city, or to look after their external affairs. Even so, monks, at the time when virtuous monks are strong, bad monks are weak. At that time, monks, the bad monks remain silent in the midst of the Saṅgha or depart in whatever direction they please. This, monks, is for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many, of devas and humans.
70:
41. "Monks, I do not praise the wrong practice (micchāpaṭipatti) of two kinds of people: the householder or the monastic. Monks, if a householder or a monastic practices wrongly, because of their wrong practice, they cannot fulfill the wholesome Dhamma of the Path along with Insight. Monks, if a householder or a monastic practices rightly, because of their right practice, they can fulfill the wholesome Dhamma of the Path along with Insight."

42. "Monks, those monks who, by means of poorly grasped discourses (suttas) with distorted phrasing, obstruct both the meaning (attha) and the Dhamma—monks, those monks act for the harm of many, for the unhappiness of many, for the ruin, harm, and suffering of many, both devas and humans. Monks, those monks generate much demerit and cause this True Dhamma (Saddhamma) to disappear. Monks, those monks who, by means of well-grasped discourses with correct phrasing, follow both the meaning and the Dhamma—monks, those monks act for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of many, both devas and humans. Monks, those monks generate much merit and sustain this True Dhamma."

The Fourth Chapter, Samacittavagga, is finished.

1. Internal fetter: Lust and desire for the realm of sensual pleasures and existence; alternatively, the lower fetters (orambhāgiya-saṃyojana).
2. External fetter: Lust and desire for the fine-material and immaterial realms; alternatively, the higher fetters (uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana).
3. Lust arising based on the five cords of sensual pleasure.
4. Lust arising based on the sixty-two types of wrong views.
5. The Pali text says 'Sāvatthī nāma nagaraṃ'. Although it is a city, it is a royal capital, so it is commonly used as 'the country of Sāvatthī'.
6. The Peit-chin (Piper longum) celestial forest.

## 5. Parisavagga

43. "Monks, there are these two kinds of assemblies. Which two? The shallow assembly and the deep assembly. Monks, what is the shallow assembly? Monks, in this teaching, in whatever assembly the monks are restless, haughty, flighty, talkative, of loose speech, unmindful, lacking clear comprehension, unconcentrated, with wandering minds and uncontrolled faculties—monks, this is called a shallow assembly. Monks, what is the deep assembly? Monks, in this teaching, in whatever assembly the monks are not restless, not haughty, not flighty, not talkative, not of loose speech, but are established in mindfulness, possess clear comprehension, are concentrated, with one-pointed minds and restrained faculties—"
71:
...possess restrained faculties. Monks, this assembly is called a deep assembly. Monks, these are the two assemblies. Monks, of these two assemblies, the deep assembly is the foremost." (1)

44. "Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The divided assembly (vagga) and the harmonious assembly (samagga). And what, monks, is the divided assembly? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks live quarrelsome, disputatious, and engaged in strife, stabbing each other with verbal daggers—this, monks, is called a divided assembly.

And what, monks, is the harmonious assembly? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks live in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputes, blending like milk and water, viewing each other with eyes of affection—this, monks, is called a harmonious assembly. Monks, these are the two assemblies. Monks, of these two assemblies, the harmonious assembly is the foremost." (2)

45. "Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The assembly not perfected in practice and the assembly perfected in practice. And what, monks, is the assembly not perfected in practice? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the senior monks are luxurious, lax, leaders in backsliding, neglecting the duty of seclusion, and do not exert effort for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. Their followers fall into the same pattern of behavior; they too become luxurious, lax, leaders in backsliding, neglecting the duty of seclusion, and do not exert effort for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This, monks, is called the assembly not perfected in practice.

And what, monks, is the assembly perfected in practice? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the senior monks are not luxurious, not lax, giving up backsliding, leaders in seclusion, and exert effort for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. Their followers fall into the same pattern of behavior; they too are not luxurious, not lax, giving up backsliding, leaders in seclusion, and exert effort for the attainment of the unattained, for the achievement of the unachieved, for the realization of the unrealized. This, monks, is called the assembly perfected in practice. Monks, these...
72:
...are the two assemblies. Monks, of these two assemblies, the assembly perfected in practice is the foremost." (3)

46. "Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The ordinary assembly and the noble assembly. And what, monks, is the ordinary assembly? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks do not understand as it really is: 'This is suffering'; they do not understand as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; they do not understand as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; they do not understand as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' This, monks, is called the ordinary assembly.

And what, monks, is the noble assembly? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks understand as it really is: 'This is suffering'; they understand as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; they understand as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; they understand as it really is: 'This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.' This, monks, is called the noble assembly. Monks, these are the two assemblies. Monks, of these two assemblies, the noble assembly is the foremost." (4)

47. "Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The assembly of dregs and the assembly of the pure. And what, monks, is the assembly of dregs? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks go the wrong way through desire, go the wrong way through hatred, go the wrong way through delusion, go the wrong way through fear. This, monks, is called the assembly of dregs.

And what, monks, is the assembly of the pure? Here, monks, in whatever assembly the monks do not go the wrong way through desire, do not go the wrong way through hatred, do not go the wrong way through delusion, do not go the wrong way through fear. This, monks, is called the assembly of the pure. Monks, these are the two assemblies. Monks, of these two assemblies, the assembly of the pure is the foremost." (5)

48. "Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The assembly trained in bombast but not in questioning, and the assembly trained in questioning but not in bombast. And what, monks, is the assembly trained in bombast but not in questioning? Here, monks, in whatever assembly, when those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata that are deep, deep in meaning, world-transcending, dealing with emptiness, are being recited, the monks do not listen well..."
73:
...they do not listen, they do not lend an ear, they do not apply their minds to knowledge, and they do not think that those teachings should be learned or mastered. But when those discourses composed by poets, poetic, with beautiful words and phrases, external, spoken by disciples, are being recited, they listen, they lend an ear, they apply their minds to knowledge, and they think that those teachings should be learned and mastered. Having learned those teachings, they do not question one another or investigate: 'How is this? What is the meaning of this?' They do not open up what is not open, they do not clarify what is not clear, and they do not dispel doubt regarding various doubt-provoking matters. This, bhikkhus, is called an assembly trained in bombast, not trained in questioning.

And what, bhikkhus, is an assembly trained in questioning, not trained in bombast? Here, bhikkhus, in whatever assembly, when those discourses composed by poets, poetic, with beautiful words and phrases, external, spoken by disciples, are being recited, the bhikkhus do not listen, do not lend an ear, do not apply their minds to knowledge, and do not think that those teachings should be learned or mastered. But when those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata, deep, deep in meaning, supramundane, connected with emptiness, are being recited, they listen, they lend an ear, they apply their minds to knowledge, and they think that those teachings should be learned. Having learned those teachings, they question one another and investigate: 'How is this? How is this? What is the meaning of this?' They open up what is not open, they clarify what is not clear, and they dispel doubt regarding various doubt-provoking matters. This, bhikkhus, is called an assembly trained in questioning, not trained in bombast. These, bhikkhus, are the two assemblies. Of these two assemblies, the assembly trained in questioning, not trained in bombast, is the foremost. (6)

49. Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The assembly that values material things, not the True Dhamma; and the assembly that values the True Dhamma, not material things. And what, bhikkhus, is the assembly that values material things, not the True Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, in whatever assembly, the bhikkhus praise one another's qualities in the presence of white-clothed laypeople, saying: 'Such a bhikkhu is one liberated in both ways; such a bhikkhu is one liberated by wisdom; such a bhikkhu is...
74:
...one liberated by wisdom; such a bhikkhu is a body-witness; such a bhikkhu is one attained to view; such a bhikkhu is one liberated by faith; such a bhikkhu is a Dhamma-follower; such a bhikkhu is a faith-follower; such a bhikkhu is virtuous, of good character; such a bhikkhu is immoral, of evil character.' Because of this, they receive gains. Having received those gains, they consume them being greedy, infatuated, and obsessed, not seeing the danger and lacking the wisdom of escape. This, bhikkhus, is called the assembly that values material things, not the True Dhamma.

And what, bhikkhus, is the assembly that values the True Dhamma, not material things? Here, bhikkhus, in whatever assembly, the bhikkhus do not praise one another's qualities in the presence of white-clothed laypeople, saying: 'Such a bhikkhu is one liberated in both ways; such a bhikkhu is one liberated by wisdom; such a bhikkhu is a body-witness; such a bhikkhu is one attained to view; such a bhikkhu is one liberated by faith; such a bhikkhu is a Dhamma-follower; such a bhikkhu is a faith-follower; such a bhikkhu is virtuous, of good character; such a bhikkhu is immoral, of evil character.' They receive gains without such praising. Having received those gains, they consume them without being greedy, infatuated, or obsessed, seeing the danger and possessing the wisdom of escape. This, bhikkhus, is called the assembly that values the True Dhamma, not material things. These, bhikkhus, are the two assemblies. Of these two assemblies, the assembly that values the True Dhamma, not material things, is the foremost. (7)

50. Bhikkhus, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The unjust assembly and the just assembly. And what, bhikkhus, is the unjust assembly? Here, bhikkhus, in whatever assembly, unlawful acts prevail and lawful acts do not prevail; acts contrary to the discipline prevail and acts in accordance with the discipline do not prevail; unlawful acts are brilliant and lawful acts are not brilliant; acts contrary to the discipline are brilliant and acts in accordance with the discipline are not brilliant. This, bhikkhus, is called the unjust assembly. 

And what, bhikkhus, is the just assembly? Here, bhikkhus, in whatever assembly, lawful acts prevail and unlawful acts do not prevail; acts in accordance with the discipline prevail and acts contrary to the discipline do not prevail; lawful acts are brilliant and unlawful acts are not brilliant; acts in accordance with the discipline are brilliant and acts contrary to the discipline are not brilliant. This, bhikkhus, is called the just assembly. These, bhikkhus, are the two assemblies. Of these two assemblies, the just assembly is the foremost. (8)
75:
51. Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The assembly that is not in accordance with the Dhamma and the assembly that is in accordance with the Dhamma... [pe]... Monks, these are the two assemblies. Of these two assemblies, the assembly that is in accordance with the Dhamma is the foremost.

52. Monks, there are these two assemblies. Which two? The assembly that speaks what is not Dhamma (Adhammavādinī) and the assembly that speaks what is Dhamma (Dhammavādinī). 

And what, monks, is the assembly that speaks what is not Dhamma? Here, monks, in an assembly where monks take up a legal issue, whether it is in accordance with the Dhamma or not. Having taken up that legal issue, they do not explain it to one another so that they may understand, nor do they assemble for the purpose of explaining it so that they may understand; they do not act to reconcile, nor do they assemble for the purpose of reconciliation. Lacking the power of understanding and the power of reconciliation, and not consulting on relinquishing the legal issue, they stubbornly cling to that very legal issue through wrong view and wrong grasping, declaring: 'This alone is the truth, everything else is empty.' This, monks, is called the assembly that speaks what is not Dhamma.

And what, monks, is the assembly that speaks what is Dhamma? Here, monks, in an assembly where monks take up a legal issue, whether it is in accordance with the Dhamma or not. Having taken up that legal issue, they explain it to one another so that they may understand and they assemble for the purpose of explaining it so that they may understand; they act to reconcile and they assemble for the purpose of reconciliation. Possessing the power of understanding and the power of reconciliation, and consulting on relinquishing the legal issue, they do not stubbornly cling to that very legal issue through wrong view and wrong grasping, declaring: 'This alone is the truth, everything else is empty.' This, monks, is called the assembly that speaks what is Dhamma. Monks, these are the two assemblies. Monks, of these two assemblies, the assembly that speaks what is Dhamma is the foremost.

The fifth chapter, the Pariṣā Vagga, is finished.
The summary of it:
Plain, Detailed, Foremost, Noble, and the fifth is Dregs;
Slanting, Material things, Uneven, and Non-Dhamma with Dhamma.
The First Fifty is finished.

(10)
The fifth chapter, the Pariṣā Vagga, is finished.
The First Fifty Suttas are finished.

The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). Monks, these two persons, when they arise in the world, arise for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of many, for gods and humans.

54. Monks, these two persons, when they arise in the world, are extraordinary humans. Which two? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). Monks, these two persons, when they arise in the world, are extraordinary humans.

55. Monks, because of the passing away of these two persons, there is regret for many people. Which two? The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and the Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti). Monks, because of the passing away of these two persons, there is regret for many people.
